data.content_ref: inline:SRC_004 argues the expert wins because 'edge cases actually determine the objective outcome,' but this is only true for tasks where edge cases dominate. Its own counterconditions concede the expert loses on routine, finite-failure-mode tasks and when the expert is prone to lapse errors. Since the problem context fixes the comparison to 'tasks with objectively verifiable outcomes'—a class that includes both routine verifiable tasks (where checklists reduce lapses) and edge-case-dominated tasks—SRC_004's universal claim ('the single domain expert will remain more reliable') is not established for the stated scope. It has no derivation or evidence to show that edge cases determine outcomes across the whole class; it merely assumes a complex-task regime. For the routine verifiable sub-class, the mechanism predicts the opposite of the claim, so the claim overgeneralizes beyond the mechanism's domain.
